cards.back: Start at the first item and compare each item in turn with the target, stopping when it is found or when the end of the list is reached and it is known to be absent.

keyPoints.text: stop when found or when the list is exhausted

mcq.correct: Start at the first item and compare each item in turn with the target, stopping when it is found or when the end of the list is reached and it is known to be absent.
distractors: Compare with the middle item and discard half the list
Sort the list first, then compare adjacent items
Compare only the first and last items

cards.explanation: Linear search needs no ordering, which is both its advantage and the reason it is slow on large lists.

cards.front: What precondition must be satisfied before binary search can be used?
cards.back: The data must already be sorted into order by the key being searched.

mcq.correct: The data must already be sorted into order by the key being searched.
distractors: The data must be stored in a linked list
The data must contain no duplicate values
The data must fit in memory twice over

cards.explanation: Discarding half the list is only valid if being greater than the middle item guarantees the target is not in the lower half.

cards.back: Compare the target with the middle item of the current range. If it matches, stop. Otherwise discard the half that cannot contain the target and repeat on the remaining half, stopping when the target is found or the range is empty.

keyPoints.text: discard the half that cannot contain the target
repeat until found or the range is empty

cards.explanation: Each step halves the search space, which is where the O(log n) complexity comes from.

cards.front: What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs on a sorted list of 1024 items?
cards.explanation: Each comparison halves the range, so the answer is log2(1024) = 10. The 512 answer comes from halving once instead of repeating.

cards.front: Why is linear search still useful when binary search is faster?
cards.back: Linear search works on unsorted data and on structures that can only be read sequentially, such as a linked list or a data stream, where jumping to the middle item is not possible.

keyPoints.text: works where random access is not available

cards.explanation: Binary search needs the middle element in constant time, so an array is fine but a linked list would cost O(n) to reach it, removing the advantage.

cards.front: Trace binary search for the value 17 in the sorted list 2, 5, 8, 12, 17, 21, 30, 44.
cards.back: Low 0, high 7, mid 3 (12): 17 is greater, so low becomes 4. Mid 5 (21): 17 is smaller, so high becomes 4. Mid 4 (17): found after 3 comparisons.

keyPoints.text: the first midpoint is index 3, value 12
17 is greater than 12 so the search moves to the upper half
the value is found at index 4

cards.explanation: The three comparisons are well inside the worst case of $\lceil\log_2 8\rceil = 3$ for a list of this size. Note that the midpoint is recomputed from the current low and high at every step rather than carried forward, and that the loop ends either on a match or when low passes high - both conditions must be handled or the search loops forever.

cards.front: What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs on a sorted list of 1,000,000 items?

synonyms: round up to the next whole comparison

keyPoints.text: each comparison halves the remaining items

cards.explanation: Each comparison halves the range, so $k$ comparisons cover $2^k$ items. Since $2^{19} = 524288$ and $2^{20} = 1048576$, twenty comparisons are needed. The contrast with linear search is the point: a million items need a million comparisons linearly and twenty by binary search.

cards.front: State the worst-case and average number of comparisons linear search makes on a list of $n$ items.
cards.back: Worst case $n$ comparisons; on average about $\frac{n}{2}$ when the item is present.

synonyms: the item is last or not present

cards.explanation: If the item is equally likely to be anywhere, the expected position is the middle, so about $\frac{n}{2}$ comparisons; if it is absent, all $n$ are made. Both figures are $O(n)$, which is why the average case does not change the complexity class - it only halves the constant. Quoting the worst case alone leaves the average unaddressed.

cards.front: Binary search is faster than linear search, so why is it unsuitable for a singly linked list?
cards.back: Binary search needs random access to jump to the middle, and reaching the middle of a linked list means walking from the start, which costs $O(n)$ and removes the advantage.

synonyms: must jump to the midpoint directly

keyPoints.text: a linked list can only be traversed from the start
finding the middle costs O(n), so the advantage is lost

mcq.correct: Linked lists have no random access, so reaching the midpoint costs $O(n)$
distractors: Linked lists cannot store sorted data
Binary search needs more memory than a linked list has
Linked lists are always too short for binary search

cards.explanation: The $O(\log n)$ bound assumes the midpoint can be reached in constant time, which is true of an array and false of a linked list. Walking to the middle each time makes each step $O(n)$ and the whole search $O(n \log n)$ - worse than the $O(n)$ linear search it was meant to replace. Data structure and algorithm have to be chosen together.

cards.front: What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs on a sorted list of 20 items?

synonyms: round log base 2 of 20 up to 5

cards.explanation: $\log_2 20 \approx 4.32$, and since a fraction of a comparison is not possible the answer rounds up to 5. Checking with powers of two is quicker than a calculator: $2^4 = 16$ covers fewer than 20 items, so four comparisons are not enough, while $2^5 = 32$ covers them comfortably. The answer 4 comes from rounding down.

cards.front: In binary search, why is the midpoint usually written `low + (high - low) // 2` rather than `(low + high) // 2`?
cards.back: They give the same result mathematically, but the first cannot overflow when `low + high` exceeds the largest representable integer.

synonyms: the sum may exceed the maximum integer
the subtraction keeps the value small

mcq.correct: To avoid overflow when `low + high` exceeds the maximum integer
distractors: It gives a different, more accurate midpoint
It is required by the language standard

cards.explanation: This was a real and famous bug: for many years the binary search in the Java standard library used `(low + high) / 2` and silently failed on arrays of more than about a billion elements. With 64-bit indices the overflow is far harder to reach, but the safe form costs nothing. It is a good example of an algorithm being correct on paper and wrong on a machine.

cards.front: How does hashing support fast searching, and what happens when two keys hash to the same place?
cards.back: A hash function maps a key to an index so a record can be found directly in $O(1)$ on average. A collision is resolved by probing for the next free slot or by chaining the records in a list at that slot.

keyPoints.text: a hash function maps the key to an index
collisions are handled by probing or chaining
synonyms: a linked list at the slot

mcq.correct: A hash gives the position directly in $O(1)$ on average; collisions use probing or chaining
distractors: A hash sorts the data so binary search can be used
A hash compresses the data so it is smaller to search
Collisions cannot occur if the hash function is good

cards.explanation: Collisions are unavoidable once there are more possible keys than slots, so a good hash function only makes them rare rather than impossible. Chaining keeps lookup $O(1)$ on average but degrades to $O(n)$ if every key collides, which is why load factor matters. Hashing also destroys ordering, so it cannot answer range queries - a binary search tree can.
